extracted.intended_audience: journalists, bloggers, media critics, and readers interested in plagiarism/ethics in journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating alleged plagiarism in journalistic writing by comparing passages, assessing attribution and edits, and judging intent and remediation. Focuses on textual similarity, editorial standards, author response, and broader public/political context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount and verbatim similarity of copied text
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the length and exactness of overlapping passages (example: Marshall’s passage is 43 words and all but one appear verbatim in Dowd’s 45-word passage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare word counts and exact matches; near‑perfect matches (all but one word identical across ~40+ words) indicate strong textual overlap even if the overall amount is not huge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of edits to the copied material
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether edits change wording and context (example: Marshall used 'we' while Dowd changed it to 'the Bush crowd').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine edits for any shift in meaning or emphasis; even minor edits can change context and are significant because journalists routinely edit quotes but should not alter meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and corrections given
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether original source was credited and whether corrections/attribution were issued (the story was corrected online and a printed correction appeared in The New York Times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check if attribution was present initially; absence increases severity. Prompt web correction and printed corrections mitigate harm and should be noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the copying could be attributed to an editorial/process error
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess if attribution was 'hacked off in the editing' or could have been lost during drafting/production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider newsroom workflows and drafting confusion as plausible explanations; if editorial removal of attribution is plausible, that reduces inference of malicious intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of the author's explanation/response
rubrics_metrics.description: How believable the author's account is (example: Dowd claimed she heard the quote from a friend and recalled a 43‑word quote with ~97% accuracy, which the author finds implausible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the plausibility of memory-based explanations, inconsistencies, and whether the response admits mistake or appears to cover it up; a believable admission lessens suspicion, while a weak explanation increases it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent versus accident
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish intentional plagiarism from accidental incorporation; weigh evidence to infer intent (amount copied, edits, and response inform this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the combination of textual evidence and response credibility to judge intent; substantial verbatim copying raises suspicion but may still be accidental; cover-up attempts shift interpretation toward intentionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic style standards on editing quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a style standard that one never edits a quote to change its meaning; edits that alter meaning violate these rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply newsroom style rules: permissible edits should not change an interviewee's meaning; violations are an ethical breach even if attribution issues are minor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when copying is present, there may be a strong fair use argument in its favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider legal/fair use defenses separately from ethical plagiarism judgments; fair use may mitigate legal liability though not necessarily ethical fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern-seeking: checking other work for additional instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators often look through an author's other writing and books for additional copying once one instance is discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single isolated incident is different from a pattern; systematic review of past work helps determine whether copying is recurring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and political/public reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of the scandal is affected by politics and schadenfreude; many reactions are driven more by political motives than by the technical severity of the copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the social and political context when judging public impact; similar amounts of copying can be amplified or downplayed depending on partisan interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (percentage) of copying relative to the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the copying as a proportion of the work (example: the author calls this 'not an egregious amount of copying by any definition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both absolute word counts and percentage of the piece; small copied passages, if properly attributed, are less ethically problematic than large unattributed sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remediation and corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions taken after discovery (web fixes, attribution, formal correction) are relevant to judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note whether the author and publisher promptly fixed the web content, gave credit, and printed a correction—these steps mitigate reputational damage and indicate responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability-based assessment of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Make probabilistic judgments about whether copying occurred and whether it was intentional (example: the author would 'confirm, with a very high level of probability, that copying did take place' but remain unclear on intent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State conclusions in terms of likelihood rather than absolute certainty when evidence is suggestive but not definitive; separate confidence in copying from confidence about motive.
